picks.rationale: Open-source Tessera model maps smallholder crops from satellite imagery at 84% accuracy with little labelled data; a peer-reviewed earth-observation/food-systems result, a field not yet covered this week.
picks.excerpt: Cambridge's open-source Tessera AI model maps smallholder crops across Senegal from satellite imagery with 84% accuracy using limited training data, 28% better than competing models at low compute cost (Environmental Research: Food Systems).

picks.rationale: GluePlex pairs AI structure prediction with physics modelling to design molecular-glue degraders without experimental structures, and the compounds were validated in cells (Nature Communications); a strong chemical-biology research result.
picks.excerpt: Baylor College of Medicine's GluePlex workflow combines AI protein-structure prediction with physics-based modeling to predict how molecular glues bind VAV1 and CRBN without experimental structures, yielding compounds that degrade VAV1 and suppress T-cell activation (Nature Communications).

picks.rationale: xECG is an xLSTM ECG foundation model trained on about 8M ECGs that beats rival models on 12-lead, long-term and smartwatch data, and the team also released the open BenchECG benchmark; the only medical pick in the set.
picks.excerpt: Medical University of Innsbruck's xECG, an xLSTM-based ECG foundation model trained on ~8 million ECGs from 1.7 million patients, outperforms rival models across classification, regression and survival tasks and handles 12-lead, long-term and smartwatch recordings; the team also released the BenchECG benchmark (npj Digital Medicine).

picks.rationale: KAIST/UNIST/POSTECH stacked ion-gated transistor layers into a reservoir-computing chip that recognises motion over time and stayed stable for 55 months (Advanced Materials); covers materials and neuromorphic hardware.
picks.excerpt: KAIST, UNIST and POSTECH built a neuromorphic reservoir-computing chip that stacks ion-gated transistor layers with fast and slow responses to recognize motion over time, reaching >90% accuracy on moving handwritten digits in simulation and staying stable for 55 months (Advanced Materials).

picks.rationale: A Harvard study finds LLMs judge trustworthiness and competence from faces, with a stronger appearance bias than humans on competence, and no model declined to judge; covers psychology and cognitive science, and it is a different study from this week's summary-memory and disagreement cards.
picks.excerpt: A Harvard study finds LLMs judge trustworthiness and competence from facial appearance like humans do, with even stronger appearance bias than people on competence, and none of the tested models declined the biased judgments.
